nature-econ-851.title: Progressive tax: rates that rise with income
nature-econ-851.text:
Under a progressive tax, the rate climbs as the taxable amount grows, so a taxpayer's average rate stays below the marginal rate. The marginal rate is the one on each extra unit of income. The effective marginal rate is higher still once lost welfare benefits and tax credits are counted. A progressive tax shifts the burden toward people with more ability to pay. Its opposite is a regressive tax, such as a sales tax, where the poor pay a larger share of income.

It directly reduces {{ref:nature-econ-850}}, especially when it funds transfers and safety nets, though more evasion at higher rates may mute the effect. Brackets that are not indexed to inflation cause bracket creep, an effective tax increase. The effect on growth is disputed. A 2008 OECD report found a weak negative relationship, while the IMF says some advanced economies could raise progressivity without hampering growth. Hayek and Nozick opposed it on principle.

nature-econ-853.title: X-inefficiency: when firms waste their own money
nature-econ-853.text: A firm can fail without any outside force pushing it: the gap between its actual cost and the lowest possible cost for its output is X-inefficiency. Harvey Leibenstein introduced it in 1966. It arises when managers lack the motivation to control costs, which is likelier without the pressure of {{ref:nature-econ-353}}, as in a monopoly or a state-owned firm. Organizational slack, using more resources than output needs, can be explained by the principal-agent problem between shareholders and managers. It concerns cost minimization, not allocative efficiency or welfare. Competition, lower entry barriers, antitrust law and better management counter it.

nature-econ-852.title: Negative income tax: paying the poor through the tax system
nature-econ-852.text: What if the tax system paid people whose income falls below a threshold? A negative income tax inverts the tax flow in this way: low earners receive payments, and those above the threshold pay tax. It is most commonly attributed to Milton Friedman and is offered as a less bureaucratic alternative to {{ref:nature-econ-851}} systems. Because subsidies adjust smoothly for poor households, it avoids the welfare trap faced by means testing.

nature-econ-855.title: Negligence: liability for failing to take care
nature-econ-855.text:
Sue a firm for fouling your land, and the claim may rest on negligence: a failure to take the care expected in similar circumstances, which makes a person liable in tort for the harm. Under common law, people have sued firms for pollution damage under {{ref:nature-econ-286}}, negligence or trespass.

Most jurisdictions require four elements: a duty of care, breach of it, actual and proximate causation, and damages. Breach is tested against what a reasonable person would have realised. Factual causation asks whether the injury would have occurred 'but for' the breach, and legal causation limits liability to harm that could reasonably be foreseen. Causation can be hard to prove, and asbestos litigation over decades has turned on it. Damages restore the victim to the original condition.

nature-econ-610.title: Common-pool resources: shared, scarce and hard to fence
nature-econ-610.text:
Each fisher on a shared ground has a reason to catch as many fish as possible before someone else does. Soon the stock runs down. Fishing grounds are a common-pool resource: a natural or human-made system that is costly, but not impossible, to keep people from using. Forests, irrigation systems, groundwater basins, pastures and the atmosphere are others.

The key is two properties met earlier. Such resources are nonexcludable like public goods, yet highly rival, because what one user takes is no longer there for others. So they get crowded or overused and suffer big multilateral negative externality problems. River water that anyone nearby can draw, and swordfish that anyone with a boat and gear can catch, are examples. So is old-growth timber in a developing country, where slow regrowth means each cut reduces what is left for others.

Ownership varies. Governments may own them as public goods, communities as common property, individuals and firms as private goods. When no one owns them they are open access. Elinor Ostrom found many run by local self-managing communities, contradicting the claim that they must be privatized or be destroyed. In James Bay, Quebec, beaver numbers recovered after Indigenous communities' customary hunting laws were legally recognized and outside trappers were banned.

nature-econ-629.title: The Coase theorem: bargaining away externalities
nature-econ-629.text:
Two radio stations interfere with each other's signals. Ronald Coase, thinking about this case, saw that the station gaining more from broadcasting would simply pay the other not to interfere. From that came the Coase theorem: when one party's activity harms or helps another, the two can bargain to an efficient outcome whoever starts with the property rights, provided bargaining costs are low enough. If fencing the farm is cheaper than fencing the cattle, a fence should go around the farm whether the farmer or the rancher holds the rights. If true, the theorem would let private individuals solve externality problems by themselves.

Coase himself did not think so. In his 1960 paper he argued that real transaction costs are rarely low enough for efficient bargaining. Imperfect information and poorly defined property rights can also block the bargain. In Danish talks between waterworks and farmers, farmers used their information advantage to seek over-compensation and drag out talks. Richard Thaler found that people care about fairness when bargaining over their own property, so they may reject efficient but unfair deals.

The starting allocation of rights does not affect efficiency, but it does affect the distribution of wealth, since the rights holder can extract payment from others. Critics argue the theorem rarely applies in practice, and Duncan Kennedy argues that the starting allocation of rights always matters.

nature-econ-879.title: Bayesian probability: belief that updates with evidence
nature-econ-879.text: Is probability a frequency or a belief? The Bayesian answer is a reasonable expectation, a state of knowledge. A Bayesian assigns a probability to a hypothesis, starting from a prior and updating it to a posterior as evidence arrives. The posterior then becomes the next prior. Objectivists treat probability as an extension of logic, subjectivists as personal belief, and the two differ mainly in how the prior is built. Decision theorists following Ramsey and von Neumann account for rational behavior with a personal probability distribution, as in the {{ref:nature-econ-797}}. Pfanzagl axiomatised subjective probability and utility.

nature-econ-878.title: Dynamic inconsistency: when today's plan fails tomorrow
nature-econ-878.text:
People tend to choose 500 dollars today over 505 tomorrow, yet 505 dollars in 366 days over 500 in 365 days. The two choices cannot both be right. This is dynamic inconsistency: preferences change over time, so an earlier plan conflicts with what the person wants later. It can be pictured as many 'selves' at different times whose preferences are not aligned. Game theorists say dynamic inconsistency, behavioral economists say time inconsistency.

{{ref:nature-econ-794}}, with a constant discount factor, yields time-consistent preferences. Empirical research suggests time inconsistency is standard in human preferences, and a stronger weight on 'now' is called the immediacy effect. See {{ref:nature-econ-748}}. Procrastination, addiction, weight loss and saving for retirement all rely on this idea.

In game theory, a player's best plan for a future period may not be optimal when it arrives, so threats lack credibility. A firm cannot commit its future self to a price war against an entrant. Commitment mechanisms limit future agency, as Odysseus did by tying himself to the mast. Independent central banks serve the same role against inflation promises (Kydland and Prescott, 1977).

nature-econ-880.title: The Ellsberg paradox: why we shun unknown odds
nature-econ-880.text:
Keynes published a version in 1921, and Daniel Ellsberg popularised it in his 1961 paper 'Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms'. In the two-urn test, urn A holds 50 red and 50 black balls and urn B an unknown mix. People are indifferent between red and black within each urn, yet strictly prefer bets on urn A. In the one-urn test, 30 of 90 balls are red and 60 are black or yellow in unknown proportion. People prefer Gamble A to B and Gamble D to C, which no single probability belief can explain.

The result holds whatever the utility function or risk aversion, because the exact odds are known for Gambles A and D but not for B and C. Most read it as {{ref:nature-econ-777}}. Choquet and maxmin expected utility are proposed responses; another explanation is deceit aversion, where people assume an unstated probability hides a trick.

nature-econ-881.title: Demurrage currency: money that melts
nature-econ-881.text:
Local stamp scrip was used in at least 450 US cities in the Great Depression, and it had a feature ordinary money lacks: it lost value on purpose. A demurrage currency loses purchasing power gradually at a constant rate. Followers of Silvio Gesell hold that money's roles as store of value and medium of exchange conflict, so money that decays is best for exchange and discourages hoarding.

Unlike {{ref:nature-econ-801}}, it reduces only the value of currency held, not newly issued money or claims such as stocks and bonds, and it does not raise consumer prices. Felix Fuders argues the growth imperative stems from interest burdens, and Bernard Lietaer says interest pushes resource use past what is ecologically optimal, such as cutting trees early. The Chiemgauer, started in Bavaria in 2003, carried a 6 percent annual rate in 2021. Keynes called stamped money sound but thought competing liquid money would evade the fees. A main barrier is trust.

nature-econ-870.title: The business cycle: booms, busts and their rhythms
nature-econ-870.text:
Economies do not grow smoothly. The business cycle is intervals of general expansion followed by recession. The simplest definition calls a recession two consecutive quarters of negative growth in {{ref:nature-econ-483}}; better ones use more indicators, such as consumer confidence, retail trade, unemployment and production indexes. Burns and Mitchell's 1946 standard definition stresses that the fluctuations are widely diffused across the economy.

Sismondi's 1819 work was the first systematic account of crises. Classical economics had denied cycles, blamed external factors such as war, or studied only the long term. Juglar first identified cycles of 7 to 11 years in 1860, and later work found Kondratiev waves in world GDP and Kuznets cycles of about 17 years. Commodity price shocks are considered a significant driver of the US cycle, and a majority of post-war recessions are linked to oil price rises. Since the 1940s most developed-nation governments have treated softening the cycle as their responsibility under stabilization policy.

nature-econ-871.title: Why economies swing: the business cycle theories
nature-econ-871.text:
Economists disagree whether business cycle fluctuations are exogenous or endogenous, that is, whether they come from outside the economy or from within it. The classical school favors outside causes and the Keynesian school inside ones. Mainstream economics sees cycles as the random summation of random causes. Slutzky's 1927 observation that summed random numbers mimic cycles led some to treat cyclicality as an artefact.

Keynesian theory says fluctuations in aggregate demand settle the economy in short-run equilibrium away from full-employment output, though Keynesian models do not necessarily imply periodic cycles. Real business cycle theory, linked to Kydland and Prescott, attributes fluctuations to random changes in total factor productivity, not monetary shocks.

Other schools blame credit. Irving Fisher's debt deflation holds that net credit expansion drives booms and bursting bubbles cause depressions. Austrian economists blame excessive bank credit, worsened by too-low central-bank rates, for a boom whose malinvestments are liquidated in the bust. Marxian theory holds that commodity production is intrinsically crisis-prone because profitability tends to fall. Kalecki's political business cycle ties cycles to resistance to sustained full employment.

nature-econ-868.title: Aggregate demand: the economy's total shopping list
nature-econ-868.text:
Aggregate demand is the total demand for final goods and services in an economy at a given time, in other words demand for a country's GDP. It is made up of consumer spending, investment, government expenditure and net exports. Consumption is modelled as C = C0 + c(Y−T), with autonomous consumption C0, marginal propensity to consume c and disposable income Y−T. Only planned investment counts. Unplanned inventory build-up signals a demand shortfall and, in the Keynesian model, falling output and income.

The curve plots real output against the price level. Its downward slope comes from Pigou's wealth effect, the Keynes interest-rate effect and the Mundell–Fleming exchange-rate effect, not from individual rational behavior. Rightward shifts come from more money supply, government spending, autonomous investment or consumption, or lower taxes. In the AD–AS model, an increase raises mainly output when resources are idle, but increasingly prices as output nears potential.

Keynes argued during the Great Depression that government spending should fill the loss of private demand. Austrian critics such as Hazlitt reject the concept as meaningless, and Hayek argued recessions have microeconomic causes.

nature-econ-872.title: Marginal propensity to consume: what an extra dollar does
nature-econ-872.text: Give someone one more dollar of disposable income and see how much they spend: that share is the marginal propensity to consume, the change in consumption divided by the change in income. With a value of 0.65, an extra dollar brings 65 cents spent and 35 saved. It is usually between 0 and 1, but can exceed 1 if the person borrows or draws down savings, and can fall below zero if higher income prompts saving for a purchase. One minus it is the marginal propensity to save in a two-sector closed economy, a key determinant of the multiplier. Keynes held it is below one, and higher for poorer people than for rich ones. The Keynesian multiplier should be larger for permanent than for temporary income changes, though telling them apart is often hard.

nature-econ-869.title: Debt and aggregate demand: the credit impulse
nature-econ-869.text: Spending equals income plus net new borrowing, so rising debt makes demand exceed income and falling debt makes it fall short. This post-Keynesian view treats changes in debt as a fundamental part of {{ref:nature-econ-868}}, sometimes called the credit impulse. The effect scales with the debt level: a 1% loan loss at 10% debt-to-GDP costs 0.1% of GDP, but at 300% of GDP costs 3%, enough to cause a recession. Write-offs and higher saving in recessions shrink credit, which can deepen the recession in a vicious cycle. The view descends from Irving Fisher's debt-deflation theory.

nature-econ-873.title: The Lorenz curve: drawing inequality
nature-econ-873.text:
Line up everyone in a country from poorest to richest, then ask how much income the bottom half holds. The Lorenz curve answers for every share at once. Max Lorenz developed it in 1905, with population share on the x-axis and income share on the y-axis. It graphs the distribution of income or wealth, as in {{ref:nature-econ-494}}. Perfect equality is the line y = x; perfect inequality, where one person has everything, is y = 0 until x = 100%. The curve runs from (0,0) to (1,1) and cannot rise above the equality line. A curve that never lies below another dominates it.

The Gini coefficient is the area between the equality line and the curve divided by the area between the equality and inequality lines. Higher means more unequal. The same device describes inequality in ecology and biodiversity studies, plotting the cumulative proportion of species against individuals.
